flagged.evidence: Step 1.2 constructs the bounded C² extension: "on [ε/2,ε] use s↦log s + log2·(1 − h(2s/ε − 1)) and on [R,2R] use s↦log s − log2·h(s/R − 1), where h(θ)=6θ^5−15θ^4+10θ^3 satisfies h=h'=h''=0 at θ=0 and h=1, h'=h''=0 at θ=1. The resulting ψ is C² with bounded first and second derivatives". It is not even C¹. On [ε/2,ε], ψ'(s) = 1/s − (2·log2/ε)·h'(2s/ε − 1), so at the inner joint ψ'(ε/2⁺) = 2/ε − (2·log2/ε)·h'(0) = 2/ε, while the branch ψ ≡ log ε on [0,ε/2] has ψ' = 0 there; on [R,2R], ψ'(2R⁻) = 1/(2R) − (log2/R)·h'(1) = 1/(2R) while the branch ψ ≡ log R on [2R,∞) has ψ' = 0 there. Hence ψ has corners at ε/2 and 2R, Φ(z)=ψ(|z−y|) is not C² with bounded derivatives, and ΔΦ = ψ''(r) + ψ'(r)/r is discontinuous at r = ε/2 and r = 2R, contrary to "its Laplacian ... is continuous and bounded". The smoothness is load-bearing: step 1.3 (Gaussian integration by parts for C² functions with bounded derivatives), step 2.2 (differentiating r ↦ Q_r f by the mean value theorem), step 3.1 (FTC applied to the continuously differentiable integrand) and step 4.1 (the martingale M_t = Φ(W_t) − Φ(W_0) − ½∫_0^t ΔΦ(W_r) dr) all consume exactly the C²_b property that fails. (Repair: interpolate with the factor (log s − log ε), e.g. ψ(s)=log ε + (log s − log ε)·h(2s/ε − 1) on [ε/2,ε], which matches value, first and second derivatives at both joints.)

Step 5.1 states "Finally B_{S_1}=D_1 and B_{S_{n+1}}=B_{S_n}+D_n, so (B_{S_1},B_{S_2},...) has the law of a simple symmetric random walk on Z started at 0", and Example item 3 likewise concludes "(B_{S_n})_{n≥1} is a simple symmetric random walk on Z started at 0". Since D_1 := B_{S_2} − B_{S_1}, the identity B_{S_1} = D_1 would force B_{S_2} = 2B_{S_1}. In fact step 2.1 makes W^{(1)} independent of F_{S_1}, so D_1 = W^{(1)}_{σ_1} is independent of the F_{S_1}-measurable B_{S_1}; both are fair signs, so P(B_{S_1} = D_1) = 1/2, not 1. Correspondingly (B_{S_n})_{n≥1} starts at B_{S_1} ∈ {−1,1}, not at 0; the walk started at 0 is (0, B_{S_1}, B_{S_2}, …) whose first step is B_{S_1} and whose later steps are the D_n. The example's actual conclusion (fairs signs, independence, SSRW law) survives once the first step is identified correctly; the defect is the displayed identity and the starting value.

Part (b) proves right-continuity with "Indeed each s>t gives F_s ⊆ F̄^0_s, so ∩_{s>t} F_s ⊆ ∩_{s>t} F̄^0_s = F_t". The first containment is false: F_s := ∩_{u>s} F̄^0_u and F̄^0 is increasing, so F̄^0_s ⊆ F̄^0_u for every u>s, giving F_s ⊇ F̄^0_s (equality only when F_s = F̄^0_s). Hence the displayed derivation of the nontrivial inclusion ∩_{s>t} F_s ⊆ F_t is invalid as written (the argument as printed yields only F_t ⊆ ∩_{s>t} F_s, which is the easy half). The asserted equality is true and follows in one line by fixing u>t and any s with t<s<u, so that F_s ⊆ F̄^0_u; the step needs that correction.

Step 3.1 begins "Fix u ≥ s, so that h := s+t−u satisfies h ≥ 0, and apply step 2.1 with base time u and horizon h in place of s and t: E[f(B_{s+t})|F^0_u] = P_h f(B_u)". The clause "so that h ≥ 0" fails whenever u > s+t (e.g. s=0, t=1, u=2 gives h=−1), and such u are within the step's own conclusion "for every u ≥ s" and are needed later by step 4.1 ("for every u > s"). Step 2.1 is stated only for horizons t ≥ 0 and the operator P_h is defined only for h ≥ 0, so the displayed inference is not licensed in that range. The conclusion is nevertheless true and is already established in the same step by the tower computation E[f(B_{s+t})|F^0_u] = E[E[f(B_{s+t})|F^0_s]|F^0_u] = P_t f(B_s), which works for every u ≥ s; deleting or restricting the first sentence repairs the step.

Step 2.2 asserts "on the other hand E_+ ⊆ {B̂_{1/(2n)} > 0} for every n ≥ 1, so P(E_+) ≤ P(B̂_{1/(2n)} > 0) = ½ by [F4]". With E_+ = ∪_m inner_m and inner_m = ∩_{r∈Q∩(0,1/m]}{B̂_r > 0} (step 1.2), the inclusion fails for small n: a path that is positive on (0,1/m] for some large m but negative at the earlier fixed time 1/(2n) lies in E_+ and not in {B̂_{1/(2n)} > 0}; such paths have positive probability. The intended bound is still correct because inner_m ⊆ {B̂_{1/(2m)} > 0} and P(E_+) = lim_m P(inner_m) ≤ ½, but the displayed set inclusion is false.

Step 1.2 defines the events through the replaced process ("E_+ := {∃ε>0: B̂_t > 0 for all t ∈ (0,ε]} and E_- := …") and concludes that they "lie in the germ sigma-algebra F^0_{0+}", citing [F2], where F^0_{0+} = ∩_{u>0} σ(B_s : 0 ≤ s ≤ u) is the germ of the raw filtration of B. The displayed argument only locates the inner events in σ(B̂_r : r ≤ 1/n). Since B̂ = B·1_{A'} with A' the measurable continuity/initial-value event (lem-brownian-motion-has-a-jointly-measurable-continuous-version), {B̂_r > 0} = A' ∩ {B_r > 0}, so E_± = A' ∩ (the B-version of E_±) and the claimed raw-germ membership is not established — the same version distinction the item's own step 2.1 correctly refuses to blur for the raw filtration. Step 2.2's appeal to Blumenthal ([F3]) is therefore not licensed as written; it becomes valid after replacing E_± by their raw-filtration counterparts, which differ by a null set and so carry the same probability.

Step 2.4 sets N := {t ∈ [a,b] : limsup_{h↓0, h∈Q} |B_{t+h} − B_t|²/h < ∞} and concludes "For every fixed deterministic t ∈ [a,b) the shifted process … is again a standard Brownian motion by [F3], so the divergence recorded in [step 1.4] holds for that t: unboundedness of the squared difference quotient along rational h↓0 is an almost-sure statement about a Brownian increment process, hence P(t∈N) = 0 for every t∈[a,b)". Step 1.4 and [F3] supply the divergence limsup_{h↓0} |B_{t+h} − B_t|²/h = +∞ only along real h; N is defined with the limsup over rational h, and the step gives no reason why the rational-h limsup is also +∞. The conclusion is true, but the needed observation — a.s. h ↦ |B_{t+h} − B_t|²/h is continuous on (0,∞) along the path, so the supremum over rational h in (0,δ) equals the supremum over real h — is not in the text and is not supplied by [F3]; without it the Fubini conclusion E λ(N) = 0 is not licensed by the stated facts.

Step 2.1 computes the complementary probability with "The events {T_3 < T_{−2}} and {T_{−2} < T_3} are disjoint, and their union has probability one because both hitting times are finite almost surely and the process cannot be at both levels at once; hence P(T_{−2} < T_3) = 1 − 2/5 = 3/5". The a.s. finiteness of T_3 and T_{−2} is the load-bearing hypothesis of the complement computation, yet it is not among the item's facts [F1]–[F3] and not among its deps (the supplier is cor-one-dimensional-brownian-motion-hits-every-point-almost-surely, which is absent); [F1] supplies only the exit probability P_x(T_b < T_a) = (x−a)/(b−a). The computation is correct once that corollary is added, so the defect is the missing support, not the value.
